proposals.hypothesis: Li2O is a wide-gap, electrically insulating binary oxide with no reducible transition metal or La/Zr cation. Its Li-rich, oxide-only composition should be chemically conservative toward LLZO and toward LiCoO2 near 4 V. It has no competing cation for self-decomposition, so it may avoid the self-decomposition penalties seen for Li2ZrO3, Li4SiO4 and Li3BO3. It is also an oxide family not yet tested in a pure form.

proposal.hypothesis: Li3PO4 is a wide-gap, electrically insulating lithium phosphate that is chemically compatible with both LLZO and LiCoO2. Its phosphate anion resists oxidation near 4 V and it is a known, effective interfacial buffer, so it should limit the reactive interphase between the two endpoints while keeping the coating insulating.

Li2ZrO3 is a wide-gap, insulating, Li-rich oxide. Its Zr(IV) matches the zirconium already in LLZO, so the LLZO contact should have little driving force for reaction. The Li-rich composition and high Li-O content should also keep it chemically stable against LiCoO2 near 4 V. Its oxide anion avoids the phosphate-driven decomposition that gave Li3PO4 a penalty of about 0.099 eV per non-Li atom.
proposal.motivation: Li3PO4 (mp-aaaaauhx) was insulating with a wide gap but had a contact penalty of 0.099 eV/non-Li atom (bin 4, not acceptable), with reaction products LaPO4, ZrO2 and O2 against LLZO. This suggests the phosphate anion is the problem, so a non-phosphate oxide is worth testing.

proposal.hypothesis: LiAlO2 is a wide-gap, insulating lithium oxide and a well-known protective coating for LiCoO2 cathodes. Its oxide anion also avoids the phosphate-driven decomposition seen with Li3PO4, and it is less Zr-rich than Li2ZrO3, which had a large self-decomposition penalty.
